issues.what: The title and alt text call the plotted values exponential data that double at each x-step, but the points follow y = 5 + 60x.
issues.why: The values increase by a constant difference of 60, not a constant factor of 2. The stated exponential model y = 5·2^x would give 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320.

issues.what: The annotation and alt text claim the points form a straight line on the semi-log plot.
issues.why: For a logarithmic y-axis, straightness requires log(y) to change linearly with x. These points have unequal successive ratios, so they do not lie on a straight line.

issues.what: The alt text says the points rise from 5 to 320, but the final plotted value is 365.
issues.why: The stated endpoint contradicts the drawing parameters.

issues.what: The plotted data series is linear rather than exponential.
issues.why: The y-values in the series are [5, 65, 125, 185, 245, 305, 365], which represent a linear progression (y = 60x + 5). On a logarithmic scale, linear data curves instead of forming a straight line. This contradicts the title, subtitle, and alt text, which all claim the plot shows exponential data (doubling from 5 to 320) appearing as a straight line.

issues.what: The alt text says the dashed line rises to the right, but its endpoints are (1, 200) and (9, 5).
issues.why: These values produce a downward-sloping straight line on a semi-log plot, opposite to the increasing scatter data.

issues.what: The claimed agreement with the dashed line and the stated early-point positions are false.
issues.why: The first two points lie below the line, not above it. The later points do not sit close to it: at x = 9, the data value is 199.5 while the line value is 5, a log10 residual of about 1.60 rather than at most 0.04.

issues.what: The dashed trend line is decreasing while the scatter data points are increasing.
issues.why: The dashed line is defined from (1, 200.0) to (9, 5.0), which slopes downward. However, the scatter points increase from 6.9 at x=1 to 199.5 at x=9. This contradicts the alt text stating that the dashed line runs up to the right and that the points sit close to it.

issues.what: The half-equivalence labels are reversed: the first is labeled “pH = pKa₂ = 9.0” and the second “pH = pKa₁ = 4.0.”
issues.why: For the specified diprotic acid, pH is approximately pKa₁ = 4.0 at 12.5 mL and pKa₂ = 9.0 at 37.5 mL. The labels contradict the specified pKa values and the alt text.

issues.what: At 8 mL, the figure labels the major species as “mostly A²⁻.”
issues.why: This is before the first half-equivalence volume of 12.5 mL, where H₂A is the major species, not A²⁻.

issues.what: At 54 mL, the figure labels the major species as “mostly H₂A.”
issues.why: This is beyond the second equivalence point at 50 mL, where the acid is predominantly fully deprotonated A²⁻, not H₂A.

issues.what: The labels for the major species along the titration curve are reversed relative to the volume of titrant added.
issues.why: At 8 mL of added base (before the first equivalence point at 25 mL), the acid is mostly in its fully protonated form, H₂A, but the label says 'mostly A²⁻'. Conversely, at 54 mL (after the second equivalence point at 50 mL), the acid is fully deprotonated to A²⁻, but the label says 'mostly H₂A'.

issues.what: The title, subtitle, alt text, and note falsely state that exponential data bend upward on a semi-log plot.
issues.why: The points satisfy y = 5 × 2^x. With a logarithmic y-axis, log(y) = log(5) + x log(2), so they form a straight line with constant slope, not an increasingly steep curve. The upward-curvature claims contradict both the drawing parameters and the entry; the note's claim that a curve indicates an exponential model is also false.

issues.what: The title, subtitle, alt text, and note assert that exponential data curves/bends upward on a semi-log plot.
issues.why: This is mathematically incorrect. On a semi-log plot (where the y-axis is logarithmically scaled), exponential data of the form y = a * b^x appears as a straight line, not a curve. This also directly contradicts the reference entry's own claim: 'when the y-axis is log-scaled, exponential data or functions appear linear.'
